Explanation: The Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) protocol was the first wireless security standard. It used a 40-bit or 104-bit key to encrypt data, but it had several weaknesses that made it vulnerable to attacks. One of these weaknesses was its use of a static encryption key, which did not change over time. This allowed attackers to capture and analyze encrypted packets to recover the key. To address this issue, the Wi-Fi Alliance introduced the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP) as part of the WPA security standard. TKIP improved upon WEP by dynamically changing the encryption key for each packet transmitted. This made it much more difficult for attackers to capture and analyze encrypted packets in order to recover the key.
